analysis.one_liner: Phases out ozone-destroying chemicals and sets binding carbon limits on cars, factories, and home equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after one subcommittee hearing on May 19, 1989, it sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee until the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Sponsored by Sen. Max Baucus with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, the bill would have phased out ozone-destroying CFCs and halons by 2000, imposed the first national carbon dioxide limits on cars (up to a 75% cut from 1985 levels by 2010) and on cement, steel, paper, and synthetic fiber plants, required efficient furnaces and air conditioners in homes, banned methane venting and flaring, and set a national goal of 50% pollution-free energy by 2000. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, received a single subcommittee hearing on May 19, 1989, and died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people. The CFC and halon phaseout would have protected the ozone layer, cutting the ultraviolet exposure the bill's own findings link to rising skin cancer rates. The vehicle, factory, and residential efficiency standards would have slowed climate change, cut smog and acid rain as a side effect, and lowered household energy bills over time. Citizen-suit provisions would have let individuals, not just regulators, enforce the rules in court.

how_it_helps.text: Phases out production of CFCs, halons, and related chemicals — frozen at 1986 levels, cut to half by 1998, and banned by 2000 except for approved medical uses — to stop stratospheric ozone depletion, which the bill's findings link to increased skin cancer and crop damage.

Sets the first binding carbon dioxide limits on cars and light trucks — 360 grams per mile for model year 1990, falling to 100 grams per mile by 2010, roughly a 75% reduction from 1985 levels — which would also have cut the smog and fine-particle pollution the bill says come from the same combustion.

Requires new and replacement furnaces, central air conditioners, and water heaters in single-family homes to meet the best available efficiency standard starting in 1992-1993, lowering household fuel and electricity use over the life of the equipment.

Gives citizens standing to sue violators in federal court and lets the EPA impose civil penalties of up to $25,000 per day and criminal penalties of up to two years' imprisonment, so enforcement does not depend entirely on agency discretion.

Requires environmental impact assessments before the U.S. votes on international development bank projects, directs the President to seek a UN program for reforestation and aid to developing nations, and requires a federal survey of highways, ports, parks, and military bases vulnerable to climate change.

analysis.who_pays: Producers of CFCs and halons, automakers, cement kilns, iron and steel operations, pulp and paper mills, synthetic fiber plants, oil and gas producers (the methane venting and flaring ban), and makers of home heating and cooling equipment. Consumers would have paid higher prices during the transition for new cars, appliances, and refrigerated goods; taxpayers would fund the groundwater recharge research program and federal vulnerability survey.
analysis.who_pays_short: CFC makers, automakers, heavy industry, oil and gas

drawbacks.text: The car standards were far beyond the technology of the day — 100 grams of carbon dioxide per mile by model year 2010, versus roughly 400 in the mid-1980s — which would have raised new-car prices and pushed buyers toward smaller vehicles, with no consumer rebate or transition assistance in the bill.

The residential equipment mandates would have raised the upfront cost of furnaces, air conditioners, and water heaters for homeowners beginning in 1992-1993, hitting households replacing a broken unit on short notice hardest.

The industrial carbon standards (25% cuts per unit of output for cement, steel, and paper; 35% for synthetic fibers) each contain an escape hatch: they lapse if the EPA Administrator merely determines the requirement is technologically infeasible.

The bill's central energy mechanism is weak: the National New Energy Development Institute it charters would be run by a board dominated by energy manufacturers and utilities, and its climate standards apply only on a voluntary basis.

The goal of 50% of U.S. energy from nonpolluting sources by 2000 was aspirational with no enforcement mechanism, and a complete CFC ban by 2000 with only narrow medical exemptions would have imposed sharp costs on refrigeration and air conditioning-dependent businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — an intact ozone layer, slower warming, lower household energy use, and enforceable citizen rights — are large and long-lasting, while the costs fall on identifiable industries and show up as transition price increases for cars and appliances. The bill's honest weaknesses are design, not intent: the car targets outran 1989 technology without transition aid, the EPA 'infeasibility' waiver could hollow out the industrial standards, and the industry-led institute's standards are voluntary where binding rules were needed. On balance, a serious, ahead-of-its-time bill whose costs were concentrated but whose protections would have been universal.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing, and died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus introduced the bill on March 17, 1989, joined by original cosponsors Sen. Dave Durenberger, a Republican, and Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Democrat.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the day it was introduced.
The committee's Subcommittee on Environmental Protection held a hearing on the bill on May 19, 1989 — the only recorded action beyond referral.
The full committee never reported the bill, the Senate never debated it, and no vote was ever taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Producers of CFCs and halons, automakers, and heavy industry kept operating without the phaseouts and emission limits; the public never received the ozone and climate protections the bill would have provided.

for.name: Max Baucus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its subcommittee held a hearing on it on May 19, 1989

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill after its one subcommittee hearing and never reported it to the Senate floor; no markup and no vote occurred

against.name: Quentin Burdick
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that held the bill without a markup or floor report

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no split can be measured; sponsorship was bipartisan — two Democrats and one Republican — and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill freezes their production at 1986 levels, cuts it to 25% by 1999, bans it by 2000 except for approved medical uses, and adds reporting, labeling, civil penalties up to $25,000 per day, and criminal exposure. Their product was the chief driver of ozone depletion, so their loss was the public's gain.

New per-mile carbon dioxide caps — 360 grams in 1990 falling to 100 grams by 2010, about a 75% cut from 1985 — would have forced the largest redesign of American vehicles ever proposed. Cheaper to comply for the industry than to pay the climate and air-quality costs, but the compliance bill lands on car prices.

industries.industry: Heavy manufacturing (cement, iron and steel, pulp and paper, synthetic fibers)
industries.note: The bill requires EPA standards cutting their carbon dioxide emissions per unit of output by 25% (35% for synthetic fibers) by 2000, unless the Administrator finds the requirement technologically infeasible. Named specifically in the bill, these industries would have borne direct capital costs.

Mass venting and flaring of methane — a standard practice at wells — is banned outright after January 1, 1994, and landfill operators face new methane-minimizing plan requirements. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, so the ban targets waste the public pays for in warming.

industries.industry: Homebuilders and heating and cooling equipment makers
industries.note: New homes from 1992 and replacement installations from 1993 could only use furnaces, central air conditioners, and water heaters meeting the best available efficiency standard. Higher upfront equipment and construction costs in exchange for lower household energy bills over time.

While other titles cut their emissions, the bill charters a National New Energy Development Institute run by a board representative of energy manufacturing industries and utilities, with federal grants up to $1 million a year, to write the nation's voluntary energy technology standards — giving the industry a formal gatekeeping seat over efficiency rules.

The bill bars the U.S. representative from voting on their projects until 120 days after a public environmental impact statement, curbing lending practices the bill says have caused deforestation and water pollution abroad.
